newsitem.title: HONG KONG: Patten--These I have loved, "1,000--year-old eggs".
newsitem.headline: Patten--These I have loved, "1,000--year-old eggs".

text.p: Maybe Chinese "1,000-year-old eggs" will arouse fond thoughts for Britain's last Hong Kong Governor Chris Patten, a gourmet, in his new post-colonial life.
They headed a "nostalgia list" he cited in pre-handover interviews during emotional hours of farewell as Britain hands Hong Kong back to China.

The avowedly-ancient eggs figure on Chinese restaurant menus, a delicacy for some, an acquired taste for others. The duck eggs, nurtured in ashes, may be a few months or years old but their taste is utterly memorable.
Patten is a well-nourished figure fond of Chinese snacks, often specially laid out for him by eager citizens on his regular meet-the-people tours.

In an interview published in Monday's South China Morning Post, he said his list would be headed by 1,000-year eggs, squawking hens and guinea fowls, and caged grasshoppers --all features of bustling Chinese market life.

"The string sacks full of frogs as black as your hat, the squirming eels, the great slabs of tuna, the wonderful fish sliced right down the middle with the life still pumping in them. Ah, what a sight," Patten told the paper.
Patten exulted about a shop he found at the top of Possession Street, where Britain planted its flag 156 years ago.
"There are thermos flasks, There are woks. There are gardening gloves. There are secaturs. All the things that make an ironmongers so much fun," Patten said.
He would also miss Andy Ng, an antique dealer in nearby Hollywood Road, who "taught me more than anybody else about Chinese arts and crafts".
And also assorted civil servants, a tennis partner, his personal assistant, the proprietor of his favourite restaurant and a chief steward who gave him horseracing tips.
Patten also said in a TV interview he had no regrets as he prepared to hand the British colony back to China and return to the anonymity of Europe to write a book.

In the talk with Hong Kong's ATV Television channel, aired just as Chinese President Jiang Zemin landed and after Patten's emotional departure from Government House, he said the time had come to let Hong Kong be run by Hong Kong people.
"I never really had any doubts about the approach that I have always taken to stand up for the people of Hong Kong," Patten said.

"It would have been a very much more difficult job if I hadn't stuck to my guns," added the outgoing governor, whose attempts to introduce limited democratic reform in Hong Kong have earned him the wrath of Beijing.
Earlier, choking back emotion, he paid his final farewells to Government House as a bugler struck up the "Last Post", a traditional military farewell sounded by a lone bugler.
His term as governor was ending at midnight (1600 GMT), when Prince Charles hands the colony to Zemin.
"It's time to go. And time for Hong Kong people to run Hong Kong," Patten said. "I shall enjoy the warm glow of anonymity."
Patten said his next job was to write a "provocative and interesting" book on Asia while recharging his batteries in the French countryside.
